So, we're still going through the language rubric. And this lesson is about writing correct, academic English.
Not perfect English. Correct, and clear. You'll see the difference in a minute.
Correctness just means using the language by its normal rules. The grammar you learned at school.
But remember... correct, not perfect. A few small slips are not what bring your score down.
So don't let perfectionism make it hard to start. Or make you write too slowly.
Just write clearly. If there's a small error here and there, that's fine. What we fix are the errors that change the meaning, and the ones that sound wrong to an academic reader.
Now, you'll notice the title says correctness and style.
In the language rubric, correctness is its own criterion. Style isn't there as a separate word, but it's actually there, inside clarity and fitting academic writing.
So what's style? It's using words, a language level, and phrasing that fit academic writing.
In English, that means no contractions, no slang, no talking to the reader as 'you', and no rhetorical questions.
And by the way, when someone writes in a style that doesn't fit academic writing, it really jars.
I mean, a rater reads academic texts all day. So when the style is different, it jumps right out.
Okay, now, the first part of correctness is common mistakes. We collected mistakes that students make again and again.
And they don't always come from weak English. Sometimes you just don't know the rule, or you didn't notice, or you had no time to proofread.
So let's go through them, so you can avoid them.
Let's start with one of the biggest sources of mistakes. Trying to sound more formal than you need to.
Some words feel formal, so people use them to make their language sound higher... and they end up with a mistake.
'Myself' sounds formal to a lot of people. But here the right word is just 'I'. 'Myself' only works when you already used 'I' in the sentence. Like, 'I taught myself'.
Same thing with 'whom'. It sounds impressive, so people put it in the wrong place. Here we need 'who'. And even better, just drop the extra words.
So if you're not sure a formal-sounding word is correct, use the simple one. It will never cost you points.
Here's another very common one. People use it every day, in emails and letters, when they want to sound a bit more official.
So what do we actually want to say here? 'If the state cancels'. So let's just write 'if'.
Because 'in case' means something else. It means as a precaution. 'Take an umbrella in case it rains'. You take the umbrella whether it rains or not.
Here too, it's 'if'. Simple. Don't complicate it.
Same goes for 'in the event that'. It isn't wrong, but it's heavy. When you mean a condition, write 'if'.
And a close relative... 'being that', as a way of saying 'because'. 'Being that these events harm residents'. That's not standard. Write 'because', or 'since'.
Now, 'due to' takes a noun. 'Due to the noise'. But before a full clause, with a subject and a verb, use 'because'.
This next one isn't a real error, but it's less accepted in academic writing.
'Plus' at the start of a sentence is spoken English. And 'Also' at the start is weak, and a bit informal.
Better to use 'In addition', 'Moreover', or 'Furthermore'.
But 'also' is totally fine inside the sentence. 'Such purchases may also lead to debt'. Just don't open the sentence with it.
Now, a mistake that comes from the way we talk. We already said, no contractions. But there's more to it.
So, full forms, of course. But look at the second fix. We didn't need 'I will demonstrate' at all. Just present the case.
Don't say the same thing twice. And that brings us to the next topic.
Redundancy. Phrases that add nothing.
'This is a complex issue.' Okay... and? How does that move forward what I want to say?
'This is not a simple dilemma.' Fine. And? It doesn't help. It doesn't add anything.
'A significant proposal.' Really.
'Logical and reasonable' is repetition. It's the same word twice.
'Good, proper and right.' We say things like that when we talk, to add emphasis. But in academic writing it doesn't fit.
And fillers. 'Basically', 'actually', 'in fact', 'literally'. 'Basically, this law is supposed to...' Why write 'basically'? Just drop it.
Some more examples, now with 'in my opinion'. This one is a classic for Hebrew speakers.
'In my opinion I think' says it twice. And 'my personal opinion'... well, obviously your opinion is personal. It's not someone else's.
'According to me' and 'according to my opinion' aren't English. They're translated word for word.
So pick one. 'In my opinion', with a comma. Or 'I believe that'. Or 'I would argue that'.
Other options are 'My view is that', or, a bit softer, 'It seems to me that'.
So where does it go? Once when you state your position, and at the start of each key sentence. Inside the development, don't repeat it. Hedge instead. Like 'may', or 'is likely to'.
Now I want to talk about fixed, 'fancy' phrases.
A lot of the time, students try to raise their language artificially, with a few fixed phrases like these.
And these are places where the formal phrase doesn't really add anything to the content.
The official guide says it clearly. Avoid flowery, needlessly difficult language. It makes the text heavy, and harder to understand.
Formal language belongs where it adds something to the content.
And I'll tell you this. If a rater sees that all your high-level words are these fixed phrases, you won't get a high language score.
The guide also asks for a uniform style. What does that mean?
Well, if you write in fairly simple, clear English, keep the whole essay in that English. Don't suddenly drop in 'it is my contention'. That makes a mixed register, and it hurts your score.
But if your whole essay is written at a high level, with rich words everywhere, then these phrases fit in. And there's no problem using them.
Spelling mistakes.
First of all, spelling isn't one of the criteria in the language rubric. Some students have dyslexia, and the test isn't meant to punish them for it.
But that's not permission to be careless. Here are some common mix-ups, for the essay, and for life in general.
'Its' without an apostrophe means belonging to it. 'It's' with an apostrophe means 'it is'. And we already said no contractions, so in the essay you almost always want 'its'.
'Affect' is usually the verb, and 'effect' is usually the noun. 'The law affects workers'. 'The law has an effect on workers'.
And watch out for pairs where both words exist, but they mean different things.
To discriminate against a group means to treat it unfairly. To distinguish between things means to tell them apart. Like distinguishing between opinion and fact.
And that one isn't really spelling anymore. It's precision. The wrong word says something you didn't mean.
